transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-30
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (ByteScale CTO), Liam O'Connor (ByteScale Backend), Zoe Kim (ByteScale SRE)

Auto-generated Summary: demo focused on long-context behavior and high-throughput streaming/backpressure; action items captured.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for making time, i'll do a 2 minute intro and then diego will jump into the edge cases demos. priya, thanks for coordinating.
[00:22] Priya Rao: thanks, maya. quick context, we're building a streaming assistant that keeps a 300k token conversation history for context windows, and we need to support bursts up to ~6k rps for small prompt types.
[00:40] Liam O'Connor: yeah, and SLOs are 200ms p50 for short prompts, we expect longer tails on the long-context flows.
[00:54] Diego Alvarez: cool, good to know. quick call out: long-context means different things - are you concatenating the whole 300k into one chunk or using summary/chunking?
[01:10] Priya Rao: we're keeping raw messages, we do some chunk-level retrieval but mostly append, which is why we wanted to see how redwood handles huge kv cache and streaming.
[01:25] Maya Chen: perfect. diego, walk them through the demo plan.
[01:30] Diego Alvarez: sure, i'll run three scenarios: 1) single large context token walk-through (simulate ~200k tokens), 2) high tps short prompts (1k-6k rps), 3) combined streaming workload that exercises backpressure and timeouts. i'll show metrics, trace snippets, and the fallback behavior.
[01:52] Zoe Kim: quick question — for private deployments, is the behavior identical or are there differences in batching/backpressure?
[02:00] Diego Alvarez: same runtime but network and instance sizing differ; with private you control autoscaler thresholds and we can add headroom to avoid queuing. hosted will do smart routing and fallbacks automatically, dedicated gives you reserved throughput to reduce tail latencies.

--- Demo scenario 1: Long context (KV/prefix caching) ---
[02:32] Diego Alvarez: starting long context demo. i'm going to send a 200k token prefix and then a short follow up prompt. watch the kv cache hits and prefix streaming.
[02:49] (screen share)
[03:10] Diego Alvarez: note — our runtime doesn't re-run the whole context per token; we stream KV cache lookups. you'll see the initial warmup is heavy, then subsequent steps are fast.
[03:28] Priya Rao: i'm seeing a big spike in memory during the 1st request, is that expected?
[03:36] Diego Alvarez: yes, memory spikes while building the kv pages, then we drop to a steady state. with quantization and 4-bit kv storage we reduce that footprint.
[03:50] Liam O'Connor: ok, can you give ballpark numbers — at 200k tokens what's the p50 and p95?
[04:02] Diego Alvarez: ballpark: p50 400-600ms for the follow up with an optimized kv path, p95 1.2-2s depending on model size and whether you hit disk. if you need <500ms tails consistently, we usually advise summarization or sharding the context and using retrieval.
[04:25] Priya Rao: we can't summarize everything, it's important to keep exact transcripts for compliance.
[04:32] Diego Alvarez: understood. in those cases we recommend dedicated pools pinned to a quantized model variant with more memory (or on-prem HBM) so you don't hit swapping.
[04:45] Zoe Kim: you mentioned disk, what storage do you use for KV pages?
[04:52] Diego Alvarez: hot KV in GPU memory, warm KV in host RAM, and cold in SSDs — we try to avoid SSD hits but for very large context sets you will see SSD in the tail. configuring sharding and pinning in dedicated reduces SSD hits.

--- Demo scenario 2: High TPS ---
[05:20] Diego Alvarez: moving to high TPS. i'll replay short prompts at ramp 500 -> 2k -> 6k rps and show throughput/latency.
[05:35] (load generator running)
[06:00] Diego Alvarez: baseline: with short context, optimized kernels and batching we can do thousands of rps per GPU for tiny completions; the numbers drop per longer output tokens. watch the autoscaler decisions.
[06:18] Liam O'Connor: what about batching latency? does batching add jitter that breaks your 200ms p50 target?
[06:26] Diego Alvarez: batching adds a small scheduling delay — usually sub 10ms to 40ms depending on batch sizes. the tradeoff is unit cost; for strict latency you can set max_batch_size=1 or use dedicated instances with lower batching thresholds.
[06:42] Priya Rao: and the autoscaler — how fast can it add GPUs on hosted?
[06:49] Maya Chen: hosted autoscaling is tuned for minutes-level scale-ups; for sudden spikes we provide burst capacity and can configure reserved headroom. Dedicated pools are best for sub-minute predictable spikes.

--- Demo scenario 3: Streaming backpressure and timeouts ---
[07:15] Diego Alvarez: now the combined streaming workload. this one will show how our streaming API handles backpressure when the consumer can't keep up. i'll simulate a slow consumer to trigger backpressure and timeouts.
[07:28] (simulation starts)
[07:45] Diego Alvarez: observe — we emit initial chunks, and when the client socket can't read fast enough we begin to apply backpressure; our runtime can buffer a small window, then we either pause generation or return an error depending on configured backpressure policy.
[08:05] Zoe Kim: what error do clients get when the buffer overruns? 429/503/504?
[08:12] Diego Alvarez: typically 502/504 for timeouts or a 429-like rate limit if you're hitting per-route quotas. we recommend client-side streaming handlers with a reconnect-and-resume strategy.
[08:25] Priya Rao: resume strategy? you can resume mid-stream?
[08:29] Diego Alvarez: yes, we support a token-offset resume that replays the last N tokens; there can be slight duplication unless you have idempotency markers. for strict ordering we recommend checkpointing decode tokens or using server-side record streaming with sequence IDs.
[08:50] Liam O'Connor: how often do you see 504s in production — is this common?
[08:56] Diego Alvarez: on hosted for customers with unpredictable bursts we see occasional 504s when downstream clients saturate their network or they don't implement backpressure handling. With dedicated and proper client retries the incidence drops to near zero.

[09:18] Priya Rao: what's Redwood's recommended retry/backoff pattern?
[09:23] Diego Alvarez: exponential backoff with jitter, start at 100ms -> 200ms -> 400ms; for streaming recommend resumable reconnects after short pauses. Avoid tight immediate retries to prevent thundering herd.
[09:36] Maya Chen: and we'll add this best-practices guide to the appendix we send.

--- Traces and dashboard walkthrough ---
[10:05] Diego Alvarez: showing sample traces — here's a trace where the client didn't read the stream and we hit backpressure, you can see the queue growth and eventual timeout at ~12s.
[10:20] Zoe Kim: can we hook this into our observability stack? e.g., get spans into our jaeger or datadog?
[10:27] Diego Alvarez: yes, we emit trace spans and logs; for Dedicated we can forward to your syslog/OTEL collector. we'll set up a Kibana/ES view for the PoC.

[11:00] Priya Rao: security questions — we need SOC2 + SSO + KMS + data residency controls. what's included?
[11:10] Diego Alvarez: we have SOC2 Type II, SAML/SSO, RBAC, tenant-level audit logs, and KMS integrations (AWS KMS/HSM). for Private deployments we support VPC peering or on-prem air-gapped installs.
[11:28] Priya Rao: do you keep request logs beyond 30 days? we have retention rules.
[11:34] Maya Chen: retention is configurable; for hosted we have defaults but you can request custom retention and we can support short retention or no retention depending on contract and Dedicated/Private choices.

--- Deep tradeoffs: Dedicated vs Hosted ---
[12:00] Diego Alvarez: quick call-out: hosted is easiest for integration and we do smart routing and fallbacks. Dedicated gives reserved GPUs, predictable throughput, and private networking. For ByteScale's workload (very long contexts + bursty spikes) Dedicated with reserved headroom plus burst pool is a common architecture.
[12:20] Priya Rao: any differences in the streaming API surface?
[12:24] Diego Alvarez: API's identical; deployment and scaling semantics differ. in Dedicated you manage autoscaler policies, but Redwood Ops can help set them initially.

--- Benchmarks & numbers ---
[12:40] Diego Alvarez: i pulled a few quick numbers from our internal bench. note these are illustrative.
[12:46] Diego Alvarez: short prompts, tiny completion: 2k-6k rps per shard with optimized kernels. long context (200k tokens) follow-up: throughput drops to ~5-50 rps per GPU depending on model size and KV hit rate. streaming with slow consumers increases tail latencies and can cause 504s if not handled.
[13:10] Priya Rao: that throughput drop is dramatic — we need to size accordingly.
[13:15] Maya Chen: yep, that's expected. we'll include the full benchmark sheet in the follow-up.
[13:22] Diego Alvarez: link: (benchmarks sheet) https://redwood-internal/benchmarks/byte-scale-demo — we'll send the access link in email.

--- Questions from ByteScale ---
[13:40] Liam O'Connor: do you support model quantization in-host for lower memory? how does that affect accuracy and latency?
[13:47] Diego Alvarez: yes, we support 4-bit quantization and a few int8 paths. 4-bit reduces memory footprint a lot, with small delta in output quality for many tasks; latency can improve because more of the model fits in HBM and avoids swapping. we do model validation to check quality.
[14:05] Priya Rao: can quantized models be used with long-context KV cache reliably?
[14:12] Diego Alvarez: yes, but you must validate specific prompt patterns — sometimes quantization amplifies subtle tokenization artifacts. we'll run a quick eval in the PoC.

--- Operational failures, fallbacks and routing ---
[14:30] Diego Alvarez: routing policies: you can set latency-based, cost-based, or region-based routes. for example, if a GPU node is overloaded we can fallback to a smaller model with lower memory to keep things responding. fallbacks are knobbed in the route config.
[14:50] Priya Rao: any risk of degraded outputs causing downstream issues if fallback to small model?
[14:56] Diego Alvarez: yes, there's always a quality vs availability tradeoff. we recommend canarying fallbacks and pairing with quality monitoring+alerts so you can auto-roll back if metrics degrade.

--- PoC proposal and instrumentation ---
[15:10] Maya Chen: proposed PoC: 2 weeks, Redwood will run a synthetic workload matching your QPS and long-context mix. we'll provide a harness, dashboards, and a security package. you provide a sample corpus and routing rules you'd like validated.
[15:28] Priya Rao: that sounds good. timeline wise we want to kick off early jan.
[15:34] Maya Chen: sounds doable. Diego will share the setup doc and we'll schedule kickoff.

--- Natural transcription artifacts / noise ---
[15:50] (background: faint typing)
[16:10] Diego Alvarez: sorry, typo — i meant 'KV cache' not 'KV kash' in the slide.
[16:18] Priya Rao: ha, no worries.

--- Follow-up: sample trace and failure mode details ---
[16:30] Diego Alvarez: i'll show a trace where we hit a backpressure-induced 504: you can see the socket write stalls, buffers exceed 64KB, and runtime returns a timeout after 12s. we recommend client-side windowing to avoid hitting that threshold; for streaming heavy workloads we also recommend chunk sizes of ~1-2KB so clients can keep up.
[17:05] Zoe Kim: how do you recommend monitoring for imminent backpressure?
[17:10] Diego Alvarez: watch queue depth, socket write latency, and upstream ACK rates; we emit all these as metrics. set alerts on queue depth > 70% and sustained socket write latency > 200ms.

--- Customer concerns about billing and cost ---
[17:40] Priya Rao: curious on pricing — is long context billed per token even when cached?
[17:46] Maya Chen: yes, billing is per-token for prompt+completion; we provide caching discounts in Dedicated via optimized plan. with KV caching you pay less because the decode work is less, but we still charge for stored context if you persist it through our storage. we'll send sample pricing scenarios.
[18:05] Liam O'Connor: and reserved capacity versus burst pricing?
[18:08] Maya Chen: reserved capacity has committed monthly spend with better unit economics and guaranteed throughput; burst is pay-as-you-go with surge rates. we'll include a cost modeling sheet.

--- Implementation specifics and SDKs ---
[18:30] Diego Alvarez: quick SDK note: we support resumable streams in the node/python sdks, and you can enable token-offset resume with resume_token param. also function calling and structured outputs are supported.
[18:45] Priya Rao: are there client libraries for go/rust?
[18:48] Diego Alvarez: official node/python and community go/rust clients; we can share enterprise-grade clients for PoC.

--- Edge cases: multi-tenant isolation & security ---
[19:05] Priya Rao: we need tenant isolation across teams; what's your model?
[19:10] Maya Chen: multi-tenant isolation uses project-level namespaces, RBAC, and encryption at rest per-tenant keys. Dedicated can map to network isolation and tenant-dedicated pools.
[19:22] Zoe Kim: request-level audit logs — can we forward to our SIEM?
[19:25] Diego Alvarez: yes, log forwarding via syslog or OTLP. we'll include sample config.

--- Live Q&A and quick clarifications ---
[20:00] Priya Rao: quick clarity — if we hit a 504 mid-stream and then reconnect, will the model continue from last token deterministically?
[20:08] Diego Alvarez: deterministic resume depends on model determinism and seed. for GPT-like models there's some nondeterminism; token-offset resume attempts to be deterministic by re-decoding from a checkpoint but small diffs can occur. we recommend idempotency markers at application layer when exact determinism is required.
[20:30] Liam O'Connor: any throttle limits on streaming connections per account?
[20:34] Maya Chen: there are per-account connection limits and per-route QPS; we can raise limits for enterprise/PoC during the trial.

--- Recap and next steps ---
[21:00] Maya Chen: recap: we'll send pricing and dedicated SKUs, diego will send SOC2 & security docs, we'll provision the benchmark harness and schedule a PoC kickoff in early jan. action items noted.
[21:18] Priya Rao: thanks everyone, please include a short runbook for dealing with streaming timeouts.
[21:25] Diego Alvarez: will do — runbook and best practices in follow-up.
[21:30] Zoe Kim: please also give us read-only access to any dashboards for the PoC.
[21:35] Maya Chen: yes, we'll set that up.

(End of recorded portion)
